cells.tense: Release is happening right now, because something has actually finished.
cells.act: make room for it without steering it
cells.ask: Take a thing in your life that has clearly finished and give it no more of tomorrow. Say nothing to anyone. Notice what the room feels like.
cells.core:
You can tell the difference between a thing that's finished and a thing you're only tired of. When something has run its course, your hands come off it, and the release doesn't have to be an announcement. The space that opens is one you no longer have to manage, because nobody is being asked to carry the ending for you.

Let it stay small: a thing in your life that is genuinely done gets no more of tomorrow — off the list, out of the conversation. Keep up with the rest exactly as you have been. What's growing underneath gets more of you when you're no longer propping up what isn't. Care can be shown by removing attention, not only by giving it.
cells.sheetLine: Let go of what's finished, gently and without a speech.
cells.verb: Letting go of what no longer serves
cells.place: In half-lit terrain, one step at a time

cells.tense: You will keep handing things over before they have had time to be finished.
cells.act: keep the session even when it feels pointless
cells.ask: Hold to a small practice daily this week, same time, same length, on the flat days and the pointless ones. Change nothing about it.
cells.core:
In uncertain territory, you tend to release early. It looks like grace from the outside — stepping back before anyone asks you to, giving something up before it can be taken. Underneath, it's bracing: you let go of things that are still alive because finishing them would mean waiting to see how they turn out, and waiting is where the ache lives.

Keeping one small practice takes the opposite route. Do it on the flat days, the pointless days, the ones where nothing is moving. What you'll find is that staying with a thing while it's uncertain is a skill, not a sentence — and the release that comes after a real finish feels like setting something down rather than dropping it.

cells.tense: You were still gripping what you had already set down, holding it long after it was over.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: Take something heavy you can't set down yet and carry it for the next hour without tightening around it. No fixing, no deciding. Just carry it.
cells.core:
In fog, you keep your hands fixed on things that are long finished. A decision gets held a week past its life; an unfinished conversation gets rehearsed in case it matters again. The effort is invisible to most people, including you — it reads as being tired all the time, or as a grip that won't come off.

You don't have to release it all at once. For the next hour, carry what's heavy without adding force — don't grip it tighter, don't pretend it's not there. Keeping something at its real weight, for one hour, is a release in slow motion, and it's one your body can actually do. Stand in it a while longer and the grip loosens without your help.

cells.tense: Something has already been let go of, and you are still talking as if you chose it.
cells.act: tend it small and ask nothing of it
cells.ask: Give ten minutes of plain attention to something you actually want to keep, with no plan for it, the way you would water a young plant. Then stop.
cells.core:
You've already set something down. The change is done — the old pattern isn't running, the decision is behind you — and your own account of it hasn't caught up. Other people have noticed the shift; you narrate it as if nothing has moved. The result is that you're caring for something no longer yours to carry, which costs more than finishing ever did.

Instead of auditing what you released, tend one thing that's still growing. Ten minutes of unplanned attention to something you actually want — the book, the walk, the person — tells you by contact what's still here. Care given to what's alive, with no schedule attached, shows you what you've already let go of, and you don't have to decide anything about it to see it.
cells.sheetLine: You've already let go. Your account hasn't caught up.
cells.verb: Letting go of what no longer serves

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my first draft was that the person's grip 'protects a wound' — the record says nothing about a wound or any past cause, so I removed it. A reader could reasonably say the Too Little cell assumes chronic holding in the body when the card may be showing only a passing stiffness; the description stays on what the holding does, not where it came from. The asks stay useful even if my read is wrong: each teaches a small move that stands on its own. The sentence that served me more than them was 'you are the one who has been holding' — it sounds knowing, so it's gone.
